content.title: Reply to Reviewer izXc
content.comment:
We would like to thank Reviewer izXc for the insightful feedbacks and the time spent in the reviewing process.

> One claim is that the method outperforms complex methods but what about simple ones: does it outperform simple methods such as Snyder 2012, Croston or Theta? What is the benefit compared to the similar approach of Smyl 2020?
>
>Regarding the novelty, the idea seems very related to Smyl 2020 who also proposes to use a holt-winter model with a RNN. Clearly they are distinct aspect of this work given that it would have less parameters (although not detailed in the related work), however the paper would clearly need to compare to this approach to justify the improvement over this very similar previous work.

We originally selected DeepAR and Deep State Space Models as reference works because the papers have been used in the industry - through Sagemaker - and have an open-source implementation - via GluonTS - available to both practitioners and researchers; this is not the case for other well-known works, as ES-RNN.
In our experiments on the Parts dataset, PES presented 2'092 (1 $\alpha$ + 1 $\theta$ for each time series) + 12 (shared Month-of-Year seasonality) = 2'104 parameters and spent on average ~1.3s per epoch for an average total training time of ~40s. As a reference, the time spent by the M4 organizers to reproduce the ES-RNN's results had been ~5/6 days. The benchmark machine for the latter results is not known, but on our side - not directly stated in the paper - we are conducting all the experiments on commercial laptops without using GPUs.

Adding more shared seasonality will result in a number of parameters increased by the seasonal period, e.g. Hour-of-Day will add 24 parameters, Day-of-Week 7, etc.
Adding the trend will increase the total number of parameters by 1'046 units (1 $\beta$ for each time series).
In the case of local seasonality - always taking Parts as an example and Month-of-Year as the only seasonality - the total number of parameters will be 14'644 (1 $\alpha$ + 1 $\theta$ + 12 for each time series) without the trend, 15'690 (1 $\alpha$ + 1 $\beta$ + 1 $\theta$ + 12 for each time series) including it.

> rather than reporting two quantile losses, most paper have converged to report CRPS (average of all quantile losses) as it is a proper scoring rule and give a better idea of overall performance

p50 and p90 had been chosen as a direct mean to compare with DeepAR and Deep State Space Models, which are the only quantile levels reported by authors. We will use CRPS in the future.

content.title: Reply to Reviewer T5jp
content.comment:
We would like to thank Reviewer T5jp for the insightful feedbacks and the time spent in the reviewing process.

> Authors only compare PES against simple baselines from 2018 and 2019, which are not currently state-of-the-art, as several dozens of recent papers achieve better performance. For example, why do not compare against the ES-RNN? This model can also target particular quantiles.

We originally selected DeepAR and Deep State Space Models as reference works because the papers have been used in the industry - through Sagemaker - and have an open-source implementation - via GluonTS - available to both practitioners and researchers; this is not the case for other well-known works, as ES-RNN.
In our experiments on the Parts dataset, PES presented 2'092 (1 $\alpha$ + 1 $\theta$ for each time series) + 12 (shared Month-of-Year seasonality) = 2'104 parameters and spent on average ~1.3s per epoch for an average total training time of ~40s. As a reference, the time spent by the M4 organizers to reproduce the ES-RNN's results had been ~5/6 days. The benchmark machine for the latter results is not known, but on our side - not directly stated in the paper - we are conducting all the experiments on commercial laptops without using GPUs.

> If the model is learning a full distribution, why not compare on more quantiles? Alternatively, use the popular CRPS metric.

p50 and p90 had been chosen as a direct mean to compare with DeepAR and Deep State Space Models, which are the only quantile levels reported by authors. We will use CRPS in the future.

> Authors claim that the model is simpler than baselines such as DeepAR. Can authors demonstrate the computational advantages of the proposed method? For example, by comparing training and inference times.

In our experiments on the Parts dataset, PES presented 2'092 (1 $\alpha$ + 1 $\theta$ for each time series) + 12 (shared Month-of-Year seasonality) = 2'104 parameters and spent on average ~1.3s per epoch for an average total training time of ~40s. In our experiments with the GluonTS implementation of DeepAR and Deep State Space Models, each architecture requested ~6 minutes to finish training on the sq,e dqtqset. We didn't measure the inference time, but a Monte Carlo simulation can be easily parallelized - even on a single CPU - to reduce it.

> Authors mentioned that the proposed cell fused the ES and RNN models. Which components of classic RNN (or LSTM, GRU) cells does the new approach use? It seems to replace the RNN cells' internal operations by the ES equations.

We didn't reuse any components of classic RNNs, we used the general RNNs idea to produce a new cell where the ES equations are the internal operations of the RNN.

> The paper does not provide any ablation study to better understand and measure each novel component's contribution.

This will be for sure a valuable addition to our work and something we are working on.

> Is the cell architecture compatible with "stacking" several layers? It seems more layers will not help improve the model's expressivity as with normal RNN cells.

That's an interesting question. We didn't study if and how we can stack together this kind of cells for the moment. It is a subject we will keep in mind for the future.

> How does the model compare to multi-quantile models? A different approach to modeling the complete distribution is to output specific quantiles. Authors should include at least one multi-quantile model (such as the MQ-CNN).

We would like to thank the reviewer for the reference. We will for sure add one of these models in future.

> It is not clear how the model incorporated exogenous variables x.

As in other architecture the exogenous variables had been concatenated with the state vector to be passed to the relevant operations. We will make it more clear next time.

content.title: Reply to Reviewer bwqD
content.comment:
We would like to thank Reviewer bwqD for the insightful feedbacks and the time spent in the reviewing process.

> (a) The problem setup is quite conventional, i.e., univariate time series forecasting. The idea of integrating different components is not new in that some works already explore this idea for advanced model architectures, e.g., [1]. The authors are expected to elaborate more on this work's contribution and novelty.  
>  
> [1] Woo, Gerald, et al. "ETSformer: Exponential Smoothing Transformers for Time-series Forecasting." arXiv preprint arXiv:2202.01381 (2022).

We would like to thank the reviewer for the reference. It is always interesting to see how the same objective can be achieved in different ways. Transformers has been for sure a breaking change over the last years (even if the community is now riding the Stable Diffusion model wave) however the architecture is still far from being "production ready". In the given reference, for example, one of the assumptions is the additive interaction between components while, in practice, many time series show a multiplicative nature (like in the demand forecasting scenario). Dealing with hierarchical time series could be difficult and inefficient, it is not clear how a shared seasonality can be learnt. Finally, this kind of architectures require an important amount of computational power - in the given reference a Nvidia A100 GPU with 40GB or 80GB of VRAM had been used to train the network - such that work had been done (and it is still ongoing) to remove complexity. In [3], for instance, the BERT's self-attention block had been completely replaced by Fourier Transform achieving the same results with an 80% gain in training speed, raising questions about the self-attention block's utility.

On our side - not directly stated in the paper - we are conducting all the experiments on commercial laptops without using GPUs. Hierarchical information, like aggregation quantity - part of the second set of experiments that we are running -, can be incorporated in a multi-task fashion or placing a SES cell at group level. In our experiments on the Parts dataset, PES presented 2'092 (1 $\alpha$ + 1 $\theta$ for each time series) + 12 (shared Month-of-Year seasonality) = 2'104 parameters and on average ~1.3s per epoch for an average total training time of ~40s.

[3] Lee-Thorp, Ainslie, Eckstein, Ontanon "FNet: Mixing Tokens with Fourier Transforms." arXiv preprint arxiv:2105.03824

> (b) The problem definition in Eq.(2) is not rigorous. For probability models, the log-likelihood is normally taken as the learning objective.
Eq.(2) is confusing in that both the density function and loss function are given.

We kindly disagree. We highlighted the difference between a common forecasting problem in Eq.(1) and a probabilistic forecasting setting. The loss function Eq.(2) is tied to the distribution laid on the observations, as we state in Sec. 4.2.

> (d) In Eq.(9), the $\theta$ parameter set is learned for each training time series, $\theta^1, \dots, \theta^N$. The question is during inference, how to handle a time series not present in the training?

We cite ourselves from the Conslusions to answer  
*As it is, PES can not be used to forecast a new time series for which no data is available. A possible workaround would be to assign to the new series a value of $\alpha$ and $\theta$ averaged over those of related time series.*

> (e) In the experiment section, is the baseline ARIMA adapted to accommodate Negative Binomial distribution?

*auto.arima* is the well-known R function which automatically discover the best fitting order for the input data. It is not adapted to accommodate Negative Binomial. The comparison is still valid since also Deep State Space Models does not use a Negative Binomial distribution.

> As this work focuses on univariate time series, it would be good to also compare with well-known univariate methods, e.g., [2].
>
>Meanwhile, it would be better to report not individual quantile loss for p50 and p90, but also the mean quantile loss of different quantile levels or Continuous Ranked Probability Score (CRPS).
>
>[2] Oreshkin, Boris N., et al. "N-BEATS: Neural basis expansion analysis for interpretable time series forecasting." International Conference on Learning Representations. 2019.

p50 and p90 had been chosen as a direct mean to compare with DeepAR and Deep State Space Models, which are the only quantile levels reported by authors. We will use CRPS in the future. DeepAR and Deep State Space Models had been chosen as reference works because the papers have been used in the industry - through Sagemaker - and have an open-source implementation - via GluonTS - available to both practitioners and researchers; this is not the case for other well-known works that are still far away from the industry.

We will try anyway to address the concerns raised within each review for the sake of discussion, postponed for too long while focusing on the practical implementation/inclusion of all the valuable comments.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper proposes PES -Probabilistic Exponential Smoothing for univariate time series forecasting.
It contains an exponential-smoothing-based cell to iteratively model time series. 
PES is also designed to generate interval and point forecasts.
The proposed method is tested on a demand forecasting task.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strong points:
   (a) Inspired by exponential smoothing methods, the proposed PES aims to integrate the level, trend, and seasonality components in the iterative modeling of time series. 
   (b) PES can provide interval forecasts, which is a meaningful extension to conventional exponential smoothing. 

Weak points: This paper has several presentation and methodology issues as follows.

(a) The problem setup is quite conventional, i.e., univariate time series forecasting. 
     The idea of integrating different components is not new in that some works already explore this idea for advanced model architectures, e.g., [1]. 
     The authors are expected to elaborate more on this work's contribution and novelty. 

[1] Woo, Gerald, et al. "ETSformer: Exponential Smoothing Transformers for Time-series Forecasting." arXiv preprint arXiv:2202.01381 (2022).

(b) The problem definition in Eq.(2) is not rigorous. For probability models, the log-likelihood is normally taken as the learning objective.  
     Eq.(2) is confusing in that both the density function and loss function are given. 

(c) In Eq.(5), $s_t$ is introduced without explicit definition, though it seems to represent seasonality from the subsequent content. 

(c) The metrics presented in Sec. 3.3 are quite standard in probabilistic forecasting. It is preferred to put this part in the experiment section.

(d) In Eq.(9), the $\theta$ parameter set is learned for each training time series, $\theta^1, \cdots, \theta^N$. The question is during inference, how to handle a time series not present in the training?

(e) In the experiment section, is the baseline ARIMA adapted to accommodate Negative Binomial distribution?

As this work focuses on univariate time series, it would be good to also compare with well-known univariate methods, e.g., [2].

Meanwhile, it would be better to report not individual quantile loss for p50 and p90, but also the mean quantile loss of different quantile levels or  Continuous Ranked Probability Score (CRPS).

[2] Oreshkin, Boris N., et al. "N-BEATS: Neural basis expansion analysis for interpretable time series forecasting." International Conference on Learning Representations. 2019.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The problem setup is quite conventional, i.e., univariate time series forecasting. The idea of integrating different components is not new in that some works already explore this idea for advanced model architectures. The evaluation is convincing enough due to the lack of baselines and metrics.

This paper proposes PES -Probabilistic Exponential Smoothing for univariate time series forecasting. 
It contains an exponential-smoothing-based cell to iteratively model time series. 
The idea is not new, as there are existing works managing to integrate trend, and seasonality components into model architectures like Transformers.
The experiment evaluation is not thorough enough to justify the advantage of the proposed method.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes PES (Probabilistic Exponential Smoothing), a novel probabilistic model that combines RNN architectures with the classic ES statistical model. The main component is the "Simple exponential smoothing cell," which has scaling and re-scaling operations with a smoothing block. PES is interpretable and simpler than baseline models. The proposed method achieves comparable results to DeepAR and DeepSSMs on the Parts dataset.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths
- Novel PES (Probabilistic Exponential Smoothing) model fuses RNN with ES.

Weaknesses
- The major weakness of the paper is the experimental setting:
	- Authors only compare PES against simple baselines from 2018 and 2019, which are not currently state-of-the-art, as several dozens of recent papers achieve better performance. For example, why do not compare against the ES-RNN? This model can also target particular quantiles.
	- Authors only used the Parts dataset, and I strongly suggest that the authors extend the results with more datasets. For example, why not include the Traffic and Electricity datasets from the DeepAr paper?
	- The model's results are weak since it cannot outperform a simple baseline such as DeepAR.
	- If the model is learning a full distribution, why not compare on more quantiles? Alternatively, use the popular CRPS metric. 
- The decomposition plot of the model is underwhelming; it seems to provide even less information than dozens of other existing models, such as the ESRNN model.
- Authors claim that the model is simpler than baselines such as DeepAR. Can authors demonstrate the computational advantages of the proposed method? For example, by comparing training and inference times.
- Authors mentioned that the proposed cell fused the ES and RNN models. Which components of classic RNN (or LSTM, GRU) cells does the new approach use? It seems to replace the RNN cells' internal operations by the ES equations.
- The paper does not provide any ablation study to better understand and measure each novel component's contribution. 
- Is the cell architecture compatible with "stacking" several layers? It seems more layers will not help improve the model's expressivity as with normal RNN cells.
- Removing the trend component will hurt the model's performance in many settings. Most hybrid and DL models keep the trend, a crucial component. For example, the only purpose of the RNN in the ESRNN model is to predict a trend.
- How does the model compare to multi-quantile models? A different approach to modeling the complete distribution is to output specific quantiles. Authors should include at least one multi-quantile model (such as the MQ-CNN).
- It is not clear how the model incorporated exogenous variables x.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- Several recent papers have explored hybrid models between Deep Learning and statistical approaches. The general architecture of PES is novel in some aspects.
- Authors should improve clarity on the description of the model. In particular, the long paragraphs of page 5 can be simplified and divided into more paragraphs, clearly explaining each operation.
content.summary_of_the_review: The proposed model's advantages are unclear: the decomposition provides less information than many existing models, the performance is comparable to or worse than simple three years old baselines, and no demonstrated computational efficiency gains. Some of the architectural designs of the model are questionable, such as removing the trend component. Finally, the experimental results seem incomplete since it includes only one dataset, two simple baselines, and few evaluation metrics.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a method to perform probabilistic forecasting that combines RNN with exponential smoothing approach. A cell is proposed that performs a simplified holt-winter model without trend. A negative binomial likelihood is associated and parameters are learned with gradient descent. The proposed model is compared against 3 baselines on one dataset for two quantile losses.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The main strength of the approach is its simplicity. The number of parameters are not given explicitly but my understanding is that they would be much less parameters than the two other parametric baselines considered.

The main weaknesses of the paper are the lack of experimental results and the lack of novelty.

Regarding the experimental results, the paper only compares on a single dataset with only three baselines and even on this single dataset, the method does not outperform the 3 baselines. This is really insufficient for analysing the benefit of any method. The paper mentions several competitions such as M3, M4 or M5. All of those datasets are potential candidates, they are also dozens of datasets publicly available in Monash repository or Gluon-ts public datasets. The set of baseline is also very small, they are lots of baselines that would be absolutely critical to evaluate this contribution. One claim is that the method outperforms complex methods but what about simple ones: does it outperform simple methods such as Snyder 2012, Croston or Theta? What is the benefit compared to the similar approach of Smyl 2020?

Regarding the novelty, the idea seems very related to Smyl 2020 who also proposes to use a holt-winter model with a RNN. Clearly they are distinct aspect of this work given that it would have less parameters (although not detailed in the related work), however the paper would clearly need to compare to this approach to justify the improvement over this very similar previous work.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The clarity of the paper is good.

The originality is low given that other work also proposed to combine seasonal methods with RNNs although in a different fashion (Smyl 2020), the precise difference from this work is not clearly detailed (the main mention appears to be "A similar approach is found in Smyl (2020) where the Holt-Winter method is employed to pre-process the data to be fed to the RNN. In our case instead the Holt-Winter method is fused inside the RNN cell." which could be much more detailed in particular spelling out clearly the cons/pros of both approaches and explained more clearly the difference).

The quality is very low given the extent of empirical results: the method is compared against 3 baselines on a single dataset where the method only performs somehow on par.

Regarding reproducibility, the author included an archive that includes both their full experimental code, I would expect the results to be reproducible although I did not try to run the code myself.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The paper novelty and experiment section is extremely lacking, I recommend rejecting the paper as such. I would recommend the author to increase the scope of their comparison, comparing against 3 baselines on 1 dataset is not enough to validate the quality of one method. Furthermore, given the similarity with Smyl 2020, I would recommend to analyze in more detail the benefit of the approach compared to this baseline.

Small additional details:
* rather than reporting two quantile losses, most paper have converged to report CRPS (average of all quantile losses) as it is a proper scoring rule and give a better idea of overall performance

content.title: PES: Probabilistic Exponential Smoothing for Time Series Forecasting
content.abstract: Time series forecasting is a common task in many industries. It helps organizations in setting goals, making plans and taking decisions. Probabilistic forecasting, in addition, summarizes the confidence over future quantities, a useful property when targeting uncertainty. This paper proposes PES - Probabilistic Exponential Smoothing -, a hybrid model for univariate time series forecasting. The contribution is two-fold: we introduce a RNN-like cell incorporating a simple exponential smoothing operator; building on this new cell we develop an intelligible and data-efficient model. The proposed solution shows several desirable characteristics; being easy to implement and fast to train, it can accommodate multiple seasonality and learn them via cross-learning. It can produce intervals as well as point-forecasts and its structure could be a valuable time series decomposition scheme. We test the PES model over a demand forecasting task on a well-known, publicly available, dataset. Finally we show that the results obtained compare favorably to the state-of-the-art.
